title: First- and Second-Order Electron Position Correlators Reveal Topological Phase Transitions
authors: Antimo Marrazzo, Christian Loer Llemit, Massimo Capone
abstract: The theory of conventional critical phenomena is built around the concepts of fluctuations and correlators of local observables. Here, we show that topological phase transitions can also be characterized through spatial and temporal two-point correlation functions associated with fluctuations of the electronic position operator. The key object is the antisymmetric part of the position-position correlation function, which yields the Chern number in the equal-time and equal-space limit. When the system is translationally invariant in space or time (the latter case corresponding to an equilibrium condition), these two-point correlators reduce to one-variable functions of the remaining variable. Remarkably, these functions are both reminiscent of critical behaviour, including divergent correlation times and lengths signalling the phase transitions. Away from these conditions, namely in non-periodic systems or genuinely dynamical processes, criticality is instead better captured by higher-order Chern-Chern correlators constructed from local or dynamical markers obtained as coincident-point limits of the position correlators. These higher-order Chern-Chern correlators can be seen as double Levi-Civita contractions of second-order position correlators, selecting the antisymmetric sector in each index pair. We substantiate this framework through numerical simulations and analytic calculations. Our results establish a general correlator-based description of topological phase transitions, applicable to crystalline, noncrystalline, equilibrium, and dynamical systems.
summary: This work develops a general framework to characterize topological phase transitions using electron position correlation functions, moving beyond traditional critical phenomena theory. By analyzing the antisymmetric components of these correlators, the authors show that the Chern number is recovered in specific limits, and the critical behavior near TPTs is governed by the decay of these correlators. This provides a robust, correlator-based diagnostic tool for diverse quantum systems.
main_problem: The paper aims to characterize topological phase transitions (TPTs) using fluctuations and correlation functions, extending the standard theory of critical phenomena.
main_result: It establishes a general correlator-based description for TPTs applicable across various physical regimes (crystalline, noncrystalline, equilibrium, and dynamical).
method: The analysis focuses on the antisymmetric part of the electron position-position correlation function, which yields the Chern number in specific limits, and introduces higher-order Chern-Chern correlators for general cases.
model_or_system: The theory is applied to condensed matter systems, using the Haldane and Qi-Wu-Zhang (QWZ) models as examples to study the transition between topological and trivial phases.
key_observables: Position-position correlation functions ($F^{(1)}$ and $F^{(2)}$), the Chern number, and higher-order Chern-Chern correlators.
important_parameters: The distance from the critical point, quantified by the Dirac fermion mass ($m = \Delta - \Delta_c$), and system parameters like the on-site term $\Delta$.
main_assumptions: The framework relies on defining appropriate limits (equal-time, equal-space, coincident-point) for the position correlators, and sometimes neglects vertex corrections in interacting systems.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the imaginary part of the position correlator ($	ext{Im } F^{(1,A)}$) for the Haldane and QWZ models across TPTs, showing characteristic exponential decays governed by the Dirac mass.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first introducing the position correlators, showing how the antisymmetric part yields the Chern number. It then analyzes the asymptotic behavior of these correlators in both real and imaginary time/space to characterize the critical divergence near TPTs, generalizing the description to higher-order correlators.
why_interesting: The use of correlation functions to diagnose topological transitions provides a powerful, general diagnostic tool that moves beyond simple gap-closing criteria, which is relevant for understanding non-equilibrium or complex many-body dynamics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Overview of the theoretical framework. While Berry-phase polarization is related to the first moment, or dipole, of the position operator, the second cumulant is related to the quantum geometric tensor and captures both electron localization, through the quantum metric, and nontrivial topology, through the Chern number. This cumulant can be interpreted as the integrated equal-time or equal-space limit of temporal and spatial autocorrelation functions of the position operator (F(1) αβ ). In equilibrium or translationally invariant settings, these correlators reduce to one-variable functions that can be analysed in the corresponding dual spaces, namely frequency and momentum. FIG. 2. Im F(1,A) xy (R) in the pristine Haldane model for rep- resentative topological (blue) and trivial (red) phases, shown in units of −Ac/4π. At the origin, the correlator repro- duces the Chern number, whereas at finite distances it de- cays to zero (see inset) according to the asymptotic form Im F(1,A) xy (r) ∝sgn(m) cos(kσ · r)e−|m|r/vF , where the Dirac fermion mass m = ∆−∆c measures the distance from the critical point, with ∆c = 4.5 for the parameters considered here. The oscillations have a period of three unit cells, set by the momentum of K′ at which the gap closes.

FIG. 3. Imaginary part of F(1,A) xy for the Haldane model near the topological phase transition (TPT) for different values of the on-site term ∆, shown in real time (left) and imaginary time (right). At t = τ = 0, Im F(1,A) xy equals the Chern number, in units of −Ac/4π. In real time, F(1,A) xy oscillates around zero, whereas in imaginary time it rapidly decays to zero. Close to the TPT, the imaginary-time decay acquires a power-law prefactor, F(1,A) xy (τ) ∼sign(m) e−2|m|τ

FIG. 4. Numerical results for the pristine Haldane model across the topological transitions from C = −1 to C = 1, showing Im F(1,A) xy (R) (left-hand panel) and Im F(1,A) xy (τ) (right-hand panels). The insets demonstrate the agreement between the numerical results and the analytical predictions for the asymptotic behavior.

FIG. 5. Numerical results for the pristine QWZ model, showing Im F(1,A) xy (R) (upper panels) and Im F(1,A) xy (τ) (lower panels). The left-hand panels correspond to the transition from C = 1 to C = 0, whereas the right-hand panels show the transition from C = −1 to C = 1, upon increasing ∆. The insets demonstrate the agreement between the numerical results and the analytical predictions for the asymptotic behaviour.
